historical_record.description: The first of the city's squares the Park Commission rebuilt after taking them over that January: from March the old macadam walks came up and new walks, lawns and planting went in to a plan chosen from several submitted.
President William McKinley broke ground for the Dewey Monument.

The Dewey Monument, a granite column of 97 feet crowned with a bronze Victory, was designed by the architect Newton J. Tharp, with the figure by the sculptor Robert I. Aitken; the Raymond Granite Company built the granite work. With the foundation the Park Commission laid, it cost $35,537.51.
President Theodore Roosevelt dedicated the Dewey Monument, commemorating the American naval victory at Manila Bay in 1898.

The Board of Park Commissioners placed the drinking fountain the Daughters of the California Pioneers were giving to Union Square just south of the Dewey Monument, on the Geary Street side, a site its architect, J. H. Von Ahnden, approved; the board had required the design's peristyle to be dropped.

The Board of Park Commissioners accepted, at no cost to the city, Dr. Lillien J. Martin's gift of a bench in memory of Fidelia Jewett, to a design by Ralph Stackpole that the Art Commission approved for the center of the block facing Post Street, provided the flower boxes around it were guarded with iron spikes.

Union Square, among the first squares the new charter put under the Park Commissioners, was remodeled: its straight walks were replaced by diagonal ones leading to a large elliptical bed in the center, where the Dewey Memorial Monument was nearly finished, with a heavy belt of shrubs on the Powell Street side.

The Board of Park Commissioners leased the space beneath Union Square to the Union Square Garage Corporation, whose bid it had accepted, to build and run a public garage there to plans by the architect Timothy L. Pflueger.

Timothy Pflueger, architect for the Union Square Garage Corporation, presented revised plans for the surface and elevations of Union Square over the planned garage, and the Board of Park Commissioners approved them.

The Board of Park Commissioners approved a plan for a Victory House in Union Square, given by the Standard Oil Company, with a stage designed by Timothy Pflueger to be built by the Treasury Department, for selling war bonds and stamps.
